entities.summary:
Vincens Lunge (died 1536), a prominent Danish-Norwegian noble, served as a key member of the Norwegian realm council (Riksråd) and represented King Christian III of Denmark in Norway during a tumultuous period marked by the Reformation and the final consolidation of Danish rule. His career unfolded amidst the collapse of the Kalmar Union and the subsequent power struggles that determined Norway's future, positioning him as a pivotal figure in the transition from an independent, if loosely governed, kingdom to a Danish province. Lunge's strategic acumen and shifting allegiances made him a central player in the political and religious conflicts that defined early 16th-century Scandinavia.

Initially arriving in Norway in 1523, Lunge quickly rose to prominence, becoming a member of the Riksråd and marrying into the powerful Smør family. He played a critical role in the Norwegian regency after King Frederick I's death in 1533, navigating the complex political landscape between Danish royal ambitions, Norwegian national interests, and the burgeoning Protestant Reformation. His early collaboration with Archbishop Olav Engelbrektsson, the last Catholic Archbishop of Nidaros and leader of the Norwegian national party, eventually gave way to bitter rivalry as Lunge increasingly aligned with Danish Protestant interests. He was instrumental in establishing Bergen as a center of Protestant influence and often acted as the de facto ruler of Western Norway, clashing frequently with the Archbishop over control of fortresses and resources.
